content.title: Response to Reviewer SC6s
content.comment:
> "The proposed solution assumes a known number of categories K, which is unrealistic and not following the definition of the SCD task ... not able to solve the SCD task."

Thanks for pointing this out. Actually, we have reported the results with unknown K in table 5 (in Appendix). When K is unknown, we first employ the GCD method (Vaze et al, CVPR 2022) to estimate K based on the visual features, for the partially supervised setting. With the estimated K, we can run our proposed method for SCD. We will further highlight this in the main text. For unsupervised setting, estimating K remains a long-standing open question. We believe exploring the K estimation methods for SCD itself is also an intriguing problem to study. 

>  "It would be better to study the effect of changing K for the unsupervised setting."

Thanks for this suggestion. As noted in the NCD/GCD literature (e.g, DTC [Han et al, 2019] and GCD [Vaze et al, 2022], the correct K typically gives the optimal results among other options. We will further explore this for SCD.

> "The Equation (2) is technically flawed. "

We believe our Equation (2) is correct and it is not technically flawed. S^c_T is a set in Equation (2), however, we do argmax over the __count__ of occurrences of each vector s_j, obtained by P_c(s_j) in cluster c, not over the elements of S^c_T (see the final line of Sec 3.2.1, below the equation). Hence, we can obtain the voted (most common) semantic name for each cluster c by Equation (2). Therefore, we believe our Equation (2) is correct and it is not technically flawed.

content.title: Response to Reviewer YLpG
content.comment:
> "The paper seems to apply the pertaining VL model to real-world recognition instead of a novel method. Since no training process is involved, all the procedures are executed on the test data."

In this paper, we (1) proposed the visual recognition task called semantic category discovery, which is closely aligned to that tackled by humans, involving assigning semantic label names to a collection of images, and which addresses limitations in current tasks; (2) propose novel solutions to semantic category discovery using non-parametric clustering and iterative refinement with pre-trained vision-language models – for the partially labelled setting, we also proposed a constrained semi-supervised k-means for more reliable cluster assignment on unlabelled data; (3) we benchmark our proposed methods on a range of evaluation settings and introduce a new semantic evaluation metric considering the continuous nature of the semantics. Our framework achieves the state-of-the-art. 
Pretrained VL model is an important component of our method, but applying a pretrained VL model alone is not possible to handle the semantic category discovery problem, which involves category discovery, semantic voting&refinement and final semantic prediction for each instance, which is not possible to prior categorization systems nor simply applying a VL model, which requires given ground-truth semantics omitting the real world challenges of semantic discovery.  
Moreover, due to the availability of large-scale pretrained vision-language models, exploring the possibility of using minimum or no training on the target data to solve the task of interest is becoming more and more intriguing and showing promise [Zhou et al 2022, Rao et al]. Hence, we believe reducing the requirement for training is not a weakness but rather a merit. 

Zhou et al, Extract Free Dense Labels from CLIP, ECCV 2022

Zhang et al, Tip-Adapter: Training-free Adaption of CLIP for Few-shot Classification, ECCV 2022

Rao et al, DenseCLIP: Language-Guided Dense Prediction with Context-Aware Prompting, CVPR 2022

> "I'm not sure whether the setting is first proposed. Maybe other open-vocabulary methods should be compared even if they involve training."

Firstly, we wish to clarify that to our knowledge, we are the first to propose the SCD problem - that of assigning semantic names to images from an unconstrained dictionary. We did our best to find applicable baselines but believe that standard CLIP-like zero-shot classification was the only fair comparison. For instance, we note that open-vocabulary detection methods (e.g ViLD, Detic etc) do not help here as they still require a finite set of candidate class names for classification. Finally, though our method does not require training, to our understanding it has not been proposed before. And, as noted by other reviewers, it is simple but effective. 

> "From the experiment results in Table 4, It seems that the proposed method did not bring a significant improvement on ImageNet-100."

We are not sure how this conclusion is drawn from Table 4 by the reviewer, as we can clearly see the notably improvements by comparing our method (row 2, 3, 4) with the baseline (row 1).  By gradually adding our initial voting step (sec 3.2.1), our iterative refinement (sec 3.2.2) and the linear assignment (sec 3.2.2), corresponding to the results in row 2,3,4 in Table 4, we can see that after adding our component the results are significantly improved. Our method (starting row 2/3/4 in Table 4) notably outperforms the k-means baseline (row 1). Our full method (row 4 in Table 4) performs the best across the board. Namely, our method outperforms the k-means baseline by 9% and 10.7% absolute points on ImageNet-100 using CLIP and DINO visual features respectively. Hence, the improvement is significant.

content.title: Response to reviewer 3Bcq
content.comment:
> The use of an off-the-shelf pre-trained CLIP model ... suffer. 

Thanks for raising this point.	CLIP is pretrained with large-scale image-text pairs obtained from the Internet, which provides weak pair-wise supervision by contrasting between the images and text scraped. Because such a weak form of supervision is easy to obtain, without requiring the high-quality class annotations, making it infeasible to quantify whether an unlabelled instance is from seen or unseen classes by CLIP. Hence, we agree that CLIP might have seen instances from some categories in the unlabelled data. However, because CLIP was not trained to classify images or discover novel classes directly, we believe it is still valid to use CLIP or other pretrained models with large-scale but perhaps noisy image-text pairs from the Internet. In the original zero-shot transfer setting of CLIP, it is also not guaranteed that the testing images are from unseen categories than the testing data (e.g., ImageNet). Meanwhile, CLIP has also been widely used in open-vocabulary detection (e.g., ViLD, Detic etc), though they do not involve category discovery, semantic voting, or refinement to name new categories.  It would be interesting to explore even weaker forms of supervision for vision-language models or ensure such models for not seeing the new classes, for SCD and other tasks considering open-vocabulary. We are optimistic that a CLIP trained such a setting can still work in our SCD method, given the scale of the training data.

> Ablation and experimental comparisons ... perform ablations.

In our experiment, we used arguably the most challenging open-vocabulary, i.e., all the nouns. We believe using a smaller vocabulary will benefit our method and lead to better results because conceptually, this will lead to a smaller search space and thus a higher chance to find the correct one. By chance, the possibility of finding a correct semantic name from a pool of N names is 1/N. When N decreases, the chance will increase. For different visual backbones, we have used different backbones in Table 4 and Table 7. We used both a self-supervised feature backbone following GCD (Vaze at al, 2022) and a weakly supervised feature backbone from CLIP. We will explore more different options in the future. 

> What happens when there is a class imbalance ... such cases?

Currently, we follow the NCD/GCD literature to use the datasets, containing both generic classification datasets and also fine-grainded datasets. We agree that long-tail distribution will bring another axis of challenge to the problem and long-tail recognition itself contains a large body of literature. Hence, more efforts will be needed to properly explore that, and we didn’t consider it in this paper. 

> The current literature looks very limited. Object discovery ... from a slightly different perspective

We agree that the suggested line of work on object discovery is also relevant and will expand the related work to include them. Due to the page limit, we mainly focused on discussing the most relevant fields of study to this work: novel/generalized category discovery(NCD/GCD) and semantic representation learning.  Particularly, we aim at predicting each unlabelled instance with a semantic name, either from seen or unseen categories, taking inspiration directly from recent studies on NCD/GCD and vision-language models. Object discovery considers the problem of localization and/or segmenting the unlabelled objects from the queried Internet data from __given categories__ (e.g., the image searching results of `Car’ by Google), while in SCD we need to discover object categories automatically and predict semantic names for them. In the object discovery (OD) literature (e.g., [A,B]), some solutions also consider grouping images into potential subclasses of the given class, but the categorization of such potential subclasses was not the focus of OD literature. OD is also often considered in the unsupervised setting [C] by exploring shared descriptors from the entire image dataset. [D] is actually a follow-up of NCD works, DTC and RankStat/AutoNovel, by adopting NCD/GCD techniques on top of FasterRCNN.

> It might be important to make the implementation available for better reproducibility.

We will make the implementation publicly available upon acceptance.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for the time they spent reviewing the manuscript and for their constructive feedback. Overall we are glad the reviewers found the task of SCD __‘worth studying for the community’__ (SC6s) and an __‘essential problem to solve’__ (3Bcq), and further that they found the method __‘though simple, interesting’__ (3Bcq) and the paper __‘clear and easy to follow’__ (YLpG). 

We have provided detailed responses to all concerns below. However, each reviewer had a small number of key concerns which we believe can all be succinctly addressed here, and we hope to clarify any serious misunderstandings as follows:


> Reviewer 3BCq, “CLIP has seen the test categories”: 

Indeed CLIP likely __has__ been exposed to images similar to the test ones. We inherit the ‘zero-shot’ terminology from CLIP itself [Radford et al., 2021], indicating that the model has not been explicitly supervised on the test categories, but rather has only had __weak supervision__ through image-caption pretraining. Our central point, however, is that even though CLIP has been exposed to images similar to the test categories, it cannot easily assign semantic names to images without being provided a limited set of candidate category names. This is the shortcoming we tackle in this paper. However, we thank the reviewer for raising this point of confusion, and we will clarify what we mean by ‘unseen’ in the paper.

> Reviewer YLpG, on novelty, including “insufficient comparison to open-vocabulary methods”:

Firstly, we wish to clarify that to our knowledge, we are the first to propose the SCD problem - that of assigning semantic names to images from an unconstrained dictionary. We did our best to find applicable baselines but believe that standard CLIP-like zero-shot classification was the only fair comparison. For instance, we note that open-vocabulary detection methods (e.g ViLD, Detic etc) do not help here as they still require a finite set of candidate class names for classification. Finally, though our method does not require training, to our understanding it has not been proposed before. And, as noted by other reviewers, it is simple but effective. 

> Reviewer SC6s, on “Equation 2 is technically flawed” and the paper “assumes a known number of categories”:

First, we highlight that Eq. 2 is not technically flawed. We are not taking the argmax over the set itself, but a __count__ of occurrences of each element in the set (see the final line of Sec 3.2.1, below the equation).

While the main paper does assume a known number of categories, Appendix A shows results when K is estimated. In the main results, we assume the number of categories following (Vaze et al, 2022a), who suggest that category number estimation and classification can be treated orthogonally. We note that Appendix A results are in the partially supervised setting; in the fully unsupervised setting, K-estimation is highly challenging with many possible valid solutions, and is in itself an intriguing research question. We thank the reviewer for raising this point.

---
Finally, given our concerns about the reviews, we decided to withdraw our submission. Hope we have addressed the concerns of all reviewers in our responses, and made our points clear about some of the misunderstandings and overlooked information in our paper. We will include constructive comments in the future iteration of our paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper takes a different path to object recognition than typical image classifications where images are mapped to one of the predefined indices (all seen) and a traditional zero-shot setting where the image is mapped to a finite (often small set) of unseen candidate classnames. The proposed method is based on parametric clustering followed by semantic refinement. Experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
+ This paper takes a different path to object recognition than typical image classifications where images are mapped to one of the predefined indices (all seen) and a specific zero-shot setting where the image is mapped to a finite (often small set) of unseen candidate classnames. This is a nicely motivated problem setup. It is important to work on this problem given the need toward moving to open-set problems in image recognition. Good to see a very exciting area under vision and language considered for the study.  

+ The idea of non-parametric clustering and semantic refinement although simple looks interesting. To my knowledge, this is the original idea for the task at hand in the paper. 

+ A performance measure used in the paper viz. soft Semantic Accuracy also looks exciting and well-suited for the task. Results show improvement over the zero-shot transfer baselines.

Weakness:
- The use of an off-the-shelf pre-trained CLIP model with a ViT-B-16 backbone is a point of serious concern. How it was ensured that the pretrained backbone has not seen test categories? If it has seen all the categories then the claims of the paper suffer.


- Ablation and experimental comparisons are weak. Ablation with the number of candidate object categories (vocabulary) vs performance might be good to see. It might be also good to consider more visual backbones and perform ablations. 


- What happens when there is a class imbalance? An empirical analysis of such a practical scenario is important to have. It is very likely that the proposed work has to deal with long-tail distributions. What happens in such cases? 

- The current literature looks very limited. Object discovery has been an active area of research in the computer vision community for example: [A] and [B] also look at the problem from a slightly different perspective:

[A] Xinlei Chen, Abhinav Shrivastava, Abhinav Gupta:
Enriching Visual Knowledge Bases via Object Discovery and Segmentation. CVPR 2014: 2035-2042

[B]  Xinlei Chen, Abhinav Shrivastava, Abhinav Gupta:
NEIL: Extracting Visual Knowledge from Web Data. ICCV 2013: 1409-1416

Also early controlled setting efforts:

[C] Gibran Fuentes Pineda, Hisashi Koga, Toshinori Watanabe:
Object Discovery by Clustering Correlated Visual Word Sets. ICPR 2010: 750-753

[D] Jiyang Zheng, Weihao Li, Jie Hong, Lars Petersson, Nick Barnes:
Towards Open-Set Object Detection and Discovery. CVPR Workshops 2022: 3960-3969

It might be worth putting the presented work in a larger context.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The problem setup is new and exciting. It is an essential problem for the community to solve. The idea of non-parametric clustering and semantic refinement although simple looks interesting. To my knowledge, this is the original idea for the task at hand in the paper. However, it is not very significant and may not have a general impact on the broader vision and language areas.

The details are provided for implementing the paper. It might be important to make the implementation available for better reproducibility. 

The paper is mostly clear. Although there are a few grammar/language errors/typos:
Section 3: where we are have no labelled -> where we have no labelled
Section 4.1 : a 100 class subset -> a 100-class subset 
Section 4.4: (righ-hand) -> (right-hand)
Conclusion: In this work we -> In this work, we 
Please proofread the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem setup is exciting and definitely something the community should address. The solution seems original to my knowledge but not something significant. Literature coverage and experiments are weak. Using pretrained CLIP without concerning what it has seen during training for zero-shot problems is a big concern for me.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Semantic Category Discovery (SCD) task where a vision-language model assigns class names to images in a dataset given a large/unconstrained taxonomy of categories as the only prior information. A non-parametric solution is also proposed, where images are firstly clustered into several candidate categories followed by a k-means style iterative refinement process to adjust the categories. Experiments show the proposed solution is significantly better than a naïve zero-shot classifier adapted from vision-language models like CLIP and ALIGN in the unsupervised setting. And it outperforms GCD [Vaze et al, 2022a] on ImageNet-100 under semi-supervised setting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#Strengths
+ The proposed SCD task is more real-world oriented, with both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings. 
+ The proposed method outperforms GCD [Vaze et al. 2020a] on ImageNet-100 under semi-supervised setting.
#Weaknesses
- The proposed solution assumes a known number of categories K, which is unrealistic and not following the definition of the SCD task. If K is unknown, the method is not able to solve the SCD task.
- It would be better to study the effect of changing K for the unsupervised setting. 
- The Equation (2) is technically flawed. $S_T^c$ is defined as a set, so all elements in the set are unique. Therefore, argmax is not going to work.
- Even assuming the $S_T^c$ is defined as the list of text embeddings, it is not clear how to break the tie for argmax in Equation (2).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: 8/10, paper presentation is clear.

Quality: 4/10, there is technical flaw for the proposed solution.

Novelty: 7/10, the proposed SCD task is somewhat novel.

Reproducibility: 7/10, the method is straightforward and builds upon existing ML modules, which could be reproduced by an experienced researcher.
content.summary_of_the_review: The major concern on the proposed solution. It assumes the number of categories is known, which doesn’t follow the definition of the SCD task. But the SCD task is worth studying for the community. Therefore, I am leaning towards reject.

content.title: Semantic Category Discovery with Vision-language Representations
content.abstract:
Object recognition is the task of identifying the category of an object in an image.
While current models report excellent performance on existing benchmarks, most fall short of the task accomplished by the human perceptual system. For instance, traditional classifiers (e.g those trained on ImageNet) only learn to map an image to a predefined class index, without revealing the actual semantic meaning of the object in the image. Meanwhile, vision-language models like CLIP are able to assign semantic class names to unseen objects in a `zero-shot' manner, though they are once again provided a predefined set of candidate names at test-time.  In this paper, we reconsider the recognition problem and bring it closer to a practical setting.  Specifically, given only a large (essentially unconstrained) taxonomy of categories as prior information, we task a vision-language model with assigning class names to all images in a dataset. We first use non-parametric methods to establish relationships between images, which allow the model to automatically narrow down the set of possible candidate names. We then propose iteratively clustering the data and voting on class names within clusters, showing that this enables a roughly 50% improvement over the baseline on ImageNet. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in a number of settings: using different taxonomies as the semantic search space; in unsupervised and partially supervised settings; as well as with coarse-grained and fine-grained evaluation datasets.
